question: What share of U.S. electricity came from nuclear power in 2025, how does that compare with its long-run share, and why do nuclear plants run so much of the time?
answer: Nuclear power supplied about 17.4% of total U.S. electricity in 2025 [E1], consistent with EIA's figure of roughly 17–18% of utility-scale generation that year [E9][E12][E8]. That is modestly below its long-run share: from 2000 through 2020 nuclear held steady near 19.5–19.8% [E1], and it has drifted down each year since 2023 (18.2% in 2023, 17.8% in 2024, 17.4% in 2025) [E1]. EIA projects this gradual decline to continue, with nuclear's generation share falling further to 12–15% by 2050 even as total nuclear capacity stays roughly stable [E8]. The decline reflects other sources (natural gas, renewables) growing faster than nuclear output, not a collapse in nuclear generation itself—the U.S. fleet of 96 reactors at 57 plants (98,441 MW capacity) has kept output resilient through "uprates" that increase capacity at existing reactors even as the number of plants has fallen since 2012 [E4]. Nuclear plants run so much of the time because, "for cost and technical reasons," they are used far more intensively than coal or gas plants: their average capacity factor in 2025 was 91%, the highest of any generating source [E2]. This reflects their role as low-marginal-cost baseload generators that utilities keep running near-continuously rather than cycling up and down with demand. question: What record did ERCOT's hourly peak load set in July 2026, which resources met it, and why do electricity prices tend to be highest in summer?
answer:
On July 22, 2026, ERCOT's hourly peak load set a new record of 91.1 GW, 6% above the previous record of 85.5 GW set August 10, 2023 [E1][E6]. The peak occurred at 6:00 p.m. CT during a heat wave and was primarily met by natural gas (48%) and solar (32%) generation [E1][E6]. This record-setting demand was part of a broader trend, as weekly average ERCOT load also hit records in the following weeks (74.5 GW for the week ending August 22, 2026), driven by sustained high temperatures and growing demand, including from data centers seeking grid interconnection [E2][E7].

Electricity prices tend to be highest in summer because total demand is high, requiring utilities to bring more expensive generation sources online to meet that increased load [E11][E18]. More broadly, prices reflect variations in demand, fuel costs, availability of energy sources, and power plant availability [E11][E13][E17]. Extreme summer temperatures raise cooling demand, which increases fuel and electricity costs, and conditions like drought or low wind can reduce cheap hydro or wind supply, adding further upward pressure on prices [E13][E17]. Wholesale prices reflect real-time supply costs and are usually higher during afternoon and early-evening peak hours, though most retail consumers pay seasonal average rates rather than experiencing these real-time fluctuations directly [E11][E18].

question: How fast has U.S. utility-scale battery storage capacity grown recently, how much was operating at the end of 2025, and which older technology has historically provided most U.S. grid storage?
answer:
U.S. utility-scale battery storage has grown very rapidly, averaging about 70% annual growth over the last three years [E1][E6]. By the end of 2025, operational battery storage capacity reached 43.6 GW [E1][E6], and growth continued into 2026, with an additional 8.3 GW added in the first half of the year to bring total capacity to nearly 52 GW [E1][E6]; operators plan roughly 54 GW more through 2028 [E1][E6]. This marks a dramatic acceleration from just a few years earlier, when total utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) power capacity was only 8,842 MW (11,105 MWh) at the end of 2022, with most of that capacity installed after 2014 [E15].

Historically, pumped-storage hydropower has been the dominant older grid-storage technology in the United States. As of 2025, total U.S. pumped-storage hydroelectric generation capacity was about 23,156 MW across 18 states, with California, Virginia, South Carolina, Michigan, and Georgia together accounting for 61% of the national total [E13][E18]. Pumped-storage systems work by pumping water uphill to a reservoir during low-demand, low-price periods and releasing it through turbines to generate electricity during peak demand, though they consume more electricity to pump than they generate, giving most facilities net negative generation balances [E11][E13][E18].

The evidence does not include a single source that directly compares total battery capacity to pumped-storage capacity or explicitly states which has "historically provided most" storage, so this conclusion is inferred from the long-standing scale and history of pumped-storage relative to the batteries' recent emergence [E11][E13][E15][E18].

question: How much uranium concentrate did the United States produce in 2025, and what steps turn mined uranium into reactor fuel?
answer:
In 2025, U.S. uranium concentrate (U3O8, or "yellowcake") production totaled 2.1 million pounds, more than triple the 2024 volume and the highest level since 2017 [E1]. Producing U3O8 is one of the first steps in making nuclear reactor fuel. After uranium ore is mined—mostly in the western United States [E11]—it goes through a milling process where uranium is extracted from the ore to produce U3O8 [E1]. The U3O8 is then processed at conversion and enrichment facilities to concentrate the fissile U-235 isotope, since natural uranium's U-235 content is too low for most reactors and must be extracted and processed before use [E1][E11]. The enriched uranium is then made into ceramic fuel pellets, which are stacked end-to-end into roughly 12-foot fuel rods and assembled into fuel assemblies for loading into a reactor core [E1][E13]. Inside the reactor, controlled nuclear fission of the uranium fuel generates heat, which produces steam to spin turbines and generate electricity [E13][E14].

Separately, 2025 also saw increased uranium exploration activity, with 1,824 exploration drill holes totaling over 1.0 million feet, up from 1,324 holes and 0.6 million feet in 2024 [E1]. The evidence does not provide further technical detail on specific conversion (e.g., UF6 processing) or enrichment methods (e.g., centrifuge technology) beyond noting these facilities are used in the fuel cycle.

question: Why has midday metered electricity demand in New York been falling, and how much solar capacity has New York added since 2018?
answer:
Midday metered electricity demand in New York ISO has been falling primarily because of rapid growth in small-scale (rooftop/behind-the-meter) solar, which is under 1 MW and not typically metered by utilities [E1][E6]. As this unmetered generation has grown, it reduces the demand utilities see during midday hours, with the effect most pronounced in early spring (March and April) when overall demand is low and solar conditions are favorable, followed by a steeper rise in demand in the late afternoon and evening as solar output fades [E1][E6]. Since this small-scale generation isn't captured by utility meters, it doesn't show up as a distinct generation source in EIA's Hourly Electric Grid Monitor, but it is assumed to be suppressing measured demand [E1][E6].

In terms of capacity growth, total solar capacity in New York — combining both small-scale and utility-scale systems — has increased by 5.6 gigawatts (GW) since 2018, with roughly half of that (about 2.8 GW) coming from small-scale solar installations [E1][E6].

question: How is most hydrogen produced in the United States today, how does electrolysis differ, and what do research papers identify as drivers of electrolytic hydrogen cost?
answer:
Nearly all commercially produced hydrogen in the United States today is made via steam-methane reforming (SMR), which reacts high-temperature steam (1,300–1,800°F) with methane—mainly from natural gas—using a catalyst to produce hydrogen, carbon monoxide, and a relatively small amount of CO2, and is used by industrial facilities and oil refineries [E1][E5]. Electrolysis differs fundamentally: it splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using an electric current, producing only those two products with no other byproducts or emissions, drawing electricity from the grid's mix of renewables, nuclear, and fossil generation; at commercial scale it is sometimes called "power-to-gas" [E1][E5]. Because producing hydrogen this way consumes more energy than the hydrogen ultimately releases, electrolytic hydrogen is best understood as an energy carrier or storage medium rather than a primary energy source [E8][E6].

Research papers identify several drivers of electrolytic ("green") hydrogen cost. Electricity price and access to low-cost/renewable power are central: off-grid wind-powered electrolysis with high wind capacity factors yields a levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) around $7/kg, whereas grid-connected electrolyzers responding to low locational marginal prices can reach LCOH near $0.5/kg [E17]. Electrolyzer capital investment cost and efficiency are also key sensitivity parameters, though combining alkaline and PEM technologies in hybrid systems yields only marginal cost benefits (at most about 1% of total production cost, or 0.057 EUR/kgH2) [E9][E14]. Additional cost-relevant factors include the ability to earn revenue from ancillary services such as frequency reserves [E10][E19], opportunity costs of consuming versus selling renewable electricity when co-located with generation [E11][E18][E21], modular electrolyzer configuration and flexible operation under variable renewable supply [E12][E23], heat integration to reduce electrical power demand [E13][E15], and stack degradation/replacement costs, which one study finds challenge the feasibility of reaching a $1/kg LCOH target through market arbitrage alone [E22]. Spatially resolved electricity pricing also affects siting and end-use hydrogen costs [E16].

question: How much of U.S. energy came from biomass in 2025, and what were the main types?
answer:
Biomass provided about 5% of total U.S. energy consumption in 2025, equal to roughly 4,853 trillion British thermal units (TBtu) [E2]. By type, the largest share was biofuels at 2,569 TBtu (53%), followed by wood and wood waste at 1,912 TBtu (39%), and municipal solid waste, animal manure, and sewage at 372 TBtu (8%) [E2][E6]. Broader biomass feedstocks include wood and wood-processing waste (firewood, wood pellets, wood chips, sawdust, and black liquor from pulp and paper mills), agricultural crops and residues (corn, soybeans, sugar cane, switchgrass, and crop/food-processing residues, mostly used for biofuels), biogenic materials in municipal solid waste, and animal manure and human sewage used to produce biogas [E3][E7].

By consuming sector, industrial use was largest at 2,317 TBtu (48%), driven mainly by wood products and paper industries using combined heat and power for process heat and self-generated electricity. Transportation followed at 1,683 TBtu (35%), reflecting biofuel use. Residential use (firewood and pellets for heating) was 372 TBtu (8%), electric power (using wood and biomass-derived wastes to generate electricity for sale) was 318 TBtu (7%), and commercial use (including biogas from sewage treatment and landfills) was 163 TBtu (3%) [E1][E8].

question: How efficient are commercial solar panels today, and what do research papers suggest about the efficiency potential of perovskite solar cells?
answer:
Commercial PV modules today reach efficiencies approaching 25% for state-of-the-art products, up from under 10% in the mid-1980s and about 15% in 2015, while experimental or niche-market cells (e.g., for satellites) have hit nearly 50% [E1][E5][E24]. Standard commercial PV cells and panels are built from individual cells that generate DC electricity, which inverters convert to AC for grid use [E2][E25].

On perovskites, research papers indicate a strong theoretical potential well above current commercial silicon efficiencies, though a gap remains between theory and demonstrated devices. Detailed-balance modeling puts the efficiency limit for single-junction perovskite cells at roughly 31%, while experimentally optimized devices have reached about 19% PCE, with optical losses (~25%), non-radiative recombination (~35%), and ohmic losses (~35%) identified as the dominant factors preventing cells from reaching that limit [E9][E15]. Other modeling work similarly finds a limiting efficiency near 29% under idealized conditions (negligible recombination, no optical losses) [E12]. More optimistic simulations suggest a realistic pathway to 30–31% efficiency using optimized built-in potentials, highly doped or ultrathin transport layers, and a perovskite bandgap around 1.4–1.5 eV, potentially making perovskites the most efficient single-junction technology [E13][E14]. Device-engineering simulations also project efficiencies above 25% with fill factors above 85% [E17].

For tandem architectures, perovskite/silicon cells show even greater promise: simulations project up to 27% efficiency [E22], spectral-splitter designs could add 2.8–6% absolute [E20], and a 2025 experimental flexible perovskite/silicon tandem achieved a certified 29.88% efficiency [E23]. All-perovskite tandems have reached experimental efficiencies up to 26.4%, with a champion device at 24.1% [E21]. However, one analysis cautions that under realistic outdoor conditions, tandem advantages over silicon alone shrink to about 14% absolute at most, tempering some of the higher lab-based projections [E16].

question: What approaches are researchers using to forecast offshore wind power, and why does forecast accuracy matter for grid operation?
answer:
Researchers use a range of machine-learning and statistical approaches to forecast offshore wind power, generally converting or supplementing numerical weather predictions (NWP) with data-driven models. question: What was the most recent large nuclear reactor completed in the United States, and what does research say about small modular reactors as an alternative?
answer:
The most recent large nuclear reactor completed in the United States is Vogtle Unit 4 at the Alvin W. On small modular reactors (SMRs, generally <300 MWe) as an alternative, research is mixed. However, more critical economic modeling finds SMRs' operating and marginal costs—not just investment costs—are the bigger barrier to viability: at manufacturer-advertised costs, SMRs are only about as profitable as costly Vogtle 3&4-level projects, and would need prices/subsidies beyond historic norms to attract private investment [E11][E16]. A techno-economic study of SMR-data center cogeneration similarly found current SMR configurations cost 49–62% more than grid power even with tax credits, becoming competitive only at very low capital costs (~$5,000/kWe) or with a carbon price of $53–64/tCO2 [E12]. question: Where is U.S. pumped-storage hydro capacity concentrated, and why do most pumped-storage plants have negative net generation?
answer:
U.S. pumped-storage hydro (PSH) capacity is concentrated in a handful of states—California (17%), Virginia (14%), South Carolina (13%), Michigan (9%), and Georgia (8%)—which together account for 61% of the roughly 23,156 MW of total U.S. PSH capacity across 18 states in 2025 [E1][E5]. The largest single facility is Bath County, Virginia, with about 2,860 MW of nameplate capacity, while the oldest and smallest is the Rocky River plant in Connecticut (1928) [E7].

Most PSH plants show negative net generation because they are energy-storage systems, not primary generators: they pump water uphill to a reservoir using grid electricity when demand and prices are low, then release it through turbines to generate electricity during peak demand—but the energy used for pumping exceeds the energy recovered on release, due to inherent round-trip losses [E1][E2][E6][E7]. EIA specifically reports "net generation" as gross generation minus the electricity consumed for pumping/charging and self-operation; since charging draws more power than discharging returns, this net figure is negative, and EIA records it as such to avoid double-counting the electricity used to charge the system against the electricity generated by the original power plants that supplied that charging power [E3][E4].

The evidence does not cover why specific states host so much PSH capacity (e.g., grid or topographic factors), only that these five states dominate the totals.

question: What share of Norway's electricity comes from hydropower, and how does a hydroelectric plant generate power?
answer:

As for how a hydroelectric plant works: water flows through a pipe called a penstock and pushes against turbine blades, spinning them to drive a generator that produces electricity; the amount of energy available depends on the water flow volume and the "head" (elevation drop) — more flow and higher head mean more electricity [E3]. In general terms, this is an application of the turbine-generator principle common to most power plants: a moving fluid (here, water) pushes blades mounted on a rotor shaft, and the generator converts that mechanical energy into electrical energy [E5]. Conventional hydro facilities come in two main types: run-of-river systems, where river current directly turns turbines, and storage systems, where dammed reservoirs release water through turbines as needed [E3]. There are also pumped-storage systems, which pump water uphill to a reservoir during low-demand periods and release it to generate power during peak demand, though these typically consume more electricity than they generate on net [E3].

The evidence provided is U.S.-specific for the mechanical/process description and does not include Norway-specific plant design details.

question: What challenges do electricity markets face as renewable penetration grows, according to research, and what example of this shows up in California's 2026 generation data?
answer:
As renewable penetration rises, research points to several interconnected market challenges: (1) revenue cannibalization, where correlated wind/solar output depresses market prices and can undercut renewables' own revenues, though this is largely a policy-design artifact (carbon pricing avoids it, subsidy/quota schemes worsen it) [E5]; (2) the need to redesign contracts and risk-sharing mechanisms as RES penetration shifts profits away from conventional generators toward renewable ones [E1]; (3) growing grid-operation complexity—congestion, voltage management, and redispatch—along with regulatory uncertainty about how new local/flexibility markets fit into existing structures [E2]; (4) wholesale market-clearing mechanisms that fail to internalize production/consumption uncertainty, motivating proposals for probabilistic local pricing [E3]; and (5) declining system inertia from non-synchronous renewables, which increases frequency-stability risk and gives conventional synchronous generators outsized market power in ancillary services markets [E4].

California's 2026 generation data illustrates the price-suppression/oversupply dynamic directly: in CAISO, utility-scale solar generation surpassed natural gas generation on 82% of days in the first five months of 2026, up sharply from just 21% of days in the same period of 2024 and 2025, as solar output rose 21% year-over-year while natural gas generation fell 60% [E12][E17]. This reflects the "duck curve" challenge described in the literature—midday solar oversupply squeezing out flexible thermal generation—and the market's response has been rapid battery buildout, with CAISO net battery storage capacity up 79% (to 16 GW) between April 2024 and April 2026, even as gas capacity stayed flat at 29 GW [E12][E17], consistent with national storage growth to nearly 52 GW by mid-2026 [E13][E18].
